body:
Changes along the course of a river

A river's longitudinal profile describes the changing elevation of its channel from its source to its mouth. Many rivers have relatively steep upper reaches and progressively gentler downstream reaches.

The changing gradient influences the relative importance of erosion, transportation and deposition. A typical river course can therefore be divided into upper, middle and lower sections.

CharacteristicUpper courseMiddle courseLower course
GradientGenerally steepModerateGenerally gentle
Principal tendencyDowncuttingLateral erosion and transportationExtensive deposition and lateral movement
ValleyNarrow and deepProgressively widerBroad floodplain
Typical featuresV-shaped valleys, gorges, waterfallsMeanders, point bars, developing floodplainsWide floodplains, levees, oxbow lakes, possible deltas

This classification describes general tendencies rather than fixed rules. A waterfall may occur downstream wherever the river encounters a sudden difference in elevation. Depositional features can develop in mountain valleys, and bank erosion remains important in the lower course.

River valleys and their development

A river valley is an elongated depression occupied or formerly occupied by a river. Its shape develops through the combined action of channel erosion, weathering and movement of material down the valley sides.

V-shaped valley

Where vertical erosion is strong, a river cuts deeply into its bed. Weathering and downslope movement gradually remove material from the adjacent slopes, producing a valley with a narrow floor and sloping sides resembling the letter V in cross-section.

V-shaped valleys are characteristic of actively incising rivers in mountainous and upland regions. They contrast with the broad floors and steep sides characteristic of glacial U-shaped valleys.

Gorge

A gorge is a particularly deep and narrow valley with very steep, sometimes nearly vertical, walls. Strong downward erosion combined with relatively limited widening can produce a gorge.

In a typical gorge, the upper and lower widths are more nearly equal than in an ordinary V-shaped valley.

Canyon

A canyon is a deep valley whose sides commonly display steep, stepped slopes. It often develops where a river cuts through horizontally arranged rock layers of differing resistance.

Canyons are commonly wider at the top than at the bottom. The Grand Canyon in the United States, carved by the Colorado River and related erosional processes, is a classic example.

Broad, flat-floored valley

Where lateral erosion and sediment accumulation become important, the valley floor widens. The river may migrate across its alluvial deposits and develop an extensive floodplain.

Waterfalls and plunge pools

A waterfall occurs where water descends abruptly over a steep step in the riverbed. Such steps may result from differences in rock resistance, geological disturbances or sudden changes in valley elevation.

A common mechanism involves resistant rock lying above less resistant rock:

  1. The less resistant rock erodes more rapidly.
  2. Undercutting creates an overhang in the resistant upper layer.
  3. Falling water and transported debris deepen a hollow at the base.
  4. The unsupported rock eventually collapses.
  5. Repeated erosion and collapse cause the waterfall to retreat upstream, sometimes leaving a gorge downstream.

The deep hollow at the foot of a waterfall is called a plunge pool. It develops through the impact of falling water and the abrasive action of sediment.

Circular or cylindrical hollows eroded into rocky riverbeds are called potholes. Pebbles trapped in small depressions may rotate under turbulent flow, gradually enlarging the hollows.

The Narmada: a structural valley and fluvial erosion

The Narmada flows westward through a rift valley between the Vindhya ranges to the north and Satpura ranges to the south. Its broad structural setting originated through faulting, rather than solely through river erosion.

However, the river has subsequently carved erosional features along its course. The Marble Rocks gorge and Dhuandhar Falls near Jabalpur in Madhya Pradesh are notable examples.

A rift valley originates through tectonic movements and faulting. A fluvial gorge develops primarily through river incision. A river may occupy a tectonically formed valley while simultaneously creating erosional landforms within it.

Prelims focus

  • Vertical erosion is generally prominent in steep upper reaches.
  • V-shaped valleys are characteristic of river incision.
  • Gorges are deep and narrow; canyons commonly have stepped walls.
  • Waterfalls may retreat upstream through repeated undercutting and collapse.
  • Marble Rocks and Dhuandhar Falls are associated with the Narmada.
  • Trap: The Narmada rift valley is not entirely a product of river erosion.

[References: NCERT, Class 7, Our Environment, reprint 2018-19, Chapter 3, p. 15; NCERT, Class 11, Fundamentals of Physical Geography, reprint 2026-27, Chapter 6, pp. 47-49; Gujarat State Board of School Textbooks, Class 11, Geography, reprint 2020, Chapter 7, pp. 48-49; NCERT, Class 11, India: Physical Environment, reprint 2025-26, Chapter 3, p. 24. Online sources consulted 27 November 2026.]

title: River Courses, Valleys, Gorges and Waterfalls

body:
Development of meanders

A meander is a pronounced bend or loop in a river channel. A series of connected bends produces the characteristic winding course of a meandering river.

Meanders commonly develop on gently sloping floodplains where rivers can erode and deposit material along relatively unconsolidated banks. Small irregularities in the channel influence water movement. Once a bend develops, differences in flow around its inner and outer sides tend to enlarge and shift it.

Erosion and deposition at a meander bend

Outer bank

The outer bank of a meander is the concave side of the bend. Stronger flow near this bank commonly causes undercutting and removal of material.

Continued erosion produces a steep bank known as a cut bank or river cliff. As the outer bank retreats, the bend expands sideways.

Inner bank

The inner bank is the convex side of the bend. Relatively weaker flow near this bank favours sediment accumulation, often producing a depositional feature called a point bar.

The gently sloping depositional surface on the inner bank is known as a slip-off slope. The simultaneous erosion of the outer bank and deposition at the inner bank cause the river channel to migrate across its valley floor.

Outer concave bank: erosion, cut bank and steep river cliff.
Inner convex bank: deposition, point bar and gentle slip-off slope.

Formation of an oxbow lake

As adjacent meander bends enlarge, the narrow strip of land separating two nearby sections of the river may become progressively smaller. This strip is known as the meander neck.

During high flow, particularly during floods, the river may breach this neck and establish a shorter course.

  1. A meander loop grows through lateral erosion and deposition.
  2. Continued erosion narrows the meander neck.
  3. The river cuts across the neck and adopts a shorter channel.
  4. Sediment accumulates near the ends of the abandoned loop.
  5. The isolated curved channel becomes an oxbow lake.

An oxbow lake commonly resembles a crescent or horseshoe. Over time, sediment and vegetation may fill the abandoned channel, leaving a marshy depression or a curved feature known as a meander scar.

The formation of an oxbow lake involves both erosion and deposition. Erosion facilitates the cutoff, while deposition may help separate the abandoned loop from the active channel.

Braided channels

A braided river contains several interconnected channels that repeatedly divide and rejoin around sediment bars and islands.

Braiding commonly develops where a river carries abundant sediment, has a variable discharge and possesses a relatively broad channel. Sediment accumulates within the channel, dividing the flow into separate branches. Further erosion and deposition change the positions of channels and bars.

A fall in discharge relative to sediment supply can favour the formation of additional channel bars. During subsequent high flows, existing bars may be eroded, relocated or enlarged.

Indian examples

  • Burhi Gandak, Bihar: Its winding channels and abandoned meander loops illustrate meandering and oxbow-lake development.
  • Brahmaputra, Assam: Its abundant sediment supply, broad valley and marked seasonal changes in discharge contribute to extensive braided channel development.

A meandering river generally has one principal winding channel. A braided river contains several active channels that repeatedly separate and reconnect. Delta distributaries, by contrast, principally carry water away from the main river towards its outlets.

Prelims focus

  • Meanders are winding channel patterns produced through lateral river activity.
  • The outer concave bank is generally erosional.
  • Point bars develop on the inner convex bank.
  • Oxbow lakes form when river bends become isolated following a cutoff.
  • The Brahmaputra in Assam displays extensive braiding.
  • Trap: A meander or oxbow lake is not explained exclusively by deposition.

[References: NCERT, Class 7, Our Environment, reprint 2018-19, Chapter 3, pp. 15-16; NCERT, Class 11, Fundamentals of Physical Geography, reprint 2026-27, Chapter 6, pp. 50-51; Gujarat State Board of School Textbooks, Class 9, Social Science, Chapter 15, pp. 115, 118-119; US National Park Service, Fluvial Features: Meandering Stream; NCERT-CIET, module kegy_20701, section Braided Channels. Online sources consulted 27 November 2026.]

title: Meanders, Oxbow Lakes and Braided River Channels

body:
Alluvial fans at mountain foothills

An alluvial fan is a fan-shaped accumulation of river sediment formed where a stream leaves a steep, confined valley and enters an open area with a gentler gradient.

Mountain streams may carry large quantities of gravel, sand, pebbles and boulders. When they emerge onto foothill plains, their gradient decreases and their flow may spread over a wider area. The resulting reduction in transporting ability encourages sediment deposition.

Continued deposition causes the fan to grow outward from the valley opening. Stream channels may shift across its surface or divide into several branches. Relatively coarse sediments generally accumulate nearer the fan's apex, while finer sediments may be carried towards its outer margins.

Alluvial fans occur in both humid and dry regions. In general, fans in humid environments tend to have gentler slopes, while those in arid and semi-arid environments may form steeper accumulations of coarse material.

Adjacent alluvial fans may merge to create a more extensive depositional plain along a mountain front.

Development of floodplains

A floodplain is a relatively flat area adjoining a river that develops through river activity and is subject to periodic inundation.

Floodplains develop through the accumulation of sediment within migrating river channels and through the deposition of sediment outside the channel during floods.

Overbank deposition

When discharge exceeds the capacity of a river channel, water spills across the surrounding land. As it spreads, its velocity and transporting ability generally decline. Suspended sediment settles across the inundated surface.

Repeated floods build successive layers of alluvium, gradually developing a relatively flat depositional surface.

Lateral channel migration

A meandering river also builds its floodplain by eroding the outer sides of bends and depositing sediment along their inner sides. As the channel moves across the valley, former channel areas become incorporated into the surrounding plain.

Consequently, a floodplain may contain both relatively coarse channel deposits and finer overbank sediments. It can also contain abandoned channels, oxbow lakes and marshy depressions.

Natural levees

A natural levee is a low, elongated ridge of sediment deposited alongside a river channel.

During a flood, water emerging from the confined channel loses transporting ability. Relatively coarse suspended material, often sand and coarse silt, settles close to the riverbanks. Finer material remains suspended longer and travels farther across the floodplain.

Successive floods gradually raise the depositional ridges beside the channel. These ridges commonly slope gently away from the river.

Areas behind natural levees may be relatively low-lying and poorly drained. Such depressions may develop into backswamps containing fine sediment and standing water.

Natural levees and point bars

FeatureLocationFormation
Natural leveeAlong riverbanksRepeated deposition from overflowing floodwater.
Point barInner side of a meander bendDeposition associated with channel flow and lateral migration.

Both are depositional features, but a natural levee is associated primarily with overbank flooding, while a point bar develops mainly within a migrating river bend.

Significance of alluvial plains in India and Gujarat

Alluvial plains often support intensive agriculture because river deposits can produce deep and fertile soils. Their relatively level surfaces also favour settlement, road construction and other economic activities.

The Northern Plains of India developed through the long-term accumulation of sediment supplied by the Indus, Ganga and Brahmaputra river systems.

Mainland Gujarat also contains extensive alluvial plains associated with rivers including the Sabarmati, Mahi, Narmada and Tapi. These illustrate the cumulative depositional work of rivers flowing from higher inland terrain towards western coastal lowlands.

However, the agricultural advantages of floodplains coexist with flood hazards, bank erosion and channel migration. Natural levees do not eliminate the possibility of flooding.

Prelims focus

  • Alluvial fans typically form where mountain streams enter gentler foothill plains.
  • Floodplains develop through overbank deposition and lateral channel migration.
  • Natural levees form through repeated sediment deposition near riverbanks during floods.
  • Levee deposits are generally coarser than sediments deposited farther across the floodplain.
  • Point bars form on inner meander bends.
  • Trap: A natural levee is formed by river deposition; an artificial embankment is constructed by humans.

[References: NCERT, Class 6, The Earth: Our Habitat, reprint 2018-19, Chapter 6, p. 43; NCERT, Class 11, Fundamentals of Physical Geography, reprint 2026-27, Chapter 6, pp. 49-51; Gujarat State Board of School Textbooks, Class 11, Geography, reprint 2020, Chapter 7, pp. 46, 49; V. N. Kulkarni, Physical Geology of Gujarat, 1985, p. 2, Government of Gujarat; US National Park Service, River Systems and Fluvial Landforms. Online sources consulted 27 November 2026.]
